analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $7.00, then increases it automatically each year with inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2004, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85 within about two months of becoming law, to $6.45 a year later, and to $7.00 the year after that. After reaching $7.00, the wage would rise automatically every year to match increases in the Consumer Price Index, so Congress would never again have to vote to stop the minimum wage from losing value to inflation. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no vote was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage — a group that skews toward adults in service and retail jobs, many supporting families — would see their pay rise roughly 36% over two years, from $5.15 to $7.00 an hour. Because the wage would then be indexed to inflation, they would keep those gains permanently instead of watching the real value erode between congressional acts, which is what had happened in the years since the last increase in 1997.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85 an hour 60 days after enactment, to $6.45 a year later, and to $7.00 the following year — an increase of roughly 36% over two years.
After reaching $7.00, the wage would rise automatically each year in step with the Consumer Price Index, so the wage floor would never again quietly lose value between congressional acts.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, hotels, agriculture, and other labor-intensive industries — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost would be passed on to customers through small price increases. Small businesses on thin margins would feel it most, though the three-step phase-in spread over two years gives them time to adjust.

drawbacks.text: Small businesses and labor-intensive employers would bear higher payroll costs, and the phase-in to $7.00 over roughly two years still represented a substantial increase in the wage floor for low-margin industries such as restaurants and retail.

Automatic annual increases tied to the Consumer Price Index would raise the minimum wage every year without a new vote of Congress, meaning lawmakers would lose the ability to pause the wage floor during an economic downturn if employers argued it was costing jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was substantial and targeted: millions of low-wage workers, disproportionately women and adults supporting families, would have received phased raises worth thousands of dollars a year, and automatic indexation would have made future raises routine rather than hostage to election-year politics. The costs were real but modest by design: the three-step phase-in gave small businesses and low-margin employers time to adjust, and the main cost passed through to consumers as small price increases in labor-intensive services. The indexation feature is a trade-off: it guarantees the wage never loses purchasing power, but in a severe recession an automatically rising wage floor could add to job pressure, a cost indexation advocates accept in exchange for not having to beg Congress for a raise every decade.

outcome.mechanism: It died quietly in committee: the House Education and the Workforce Committee referred it to a subcommittee on workforce protections, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Chris Bell introduced the bill on September 9, 2004, with Richard Neal of Massachusetts joining as the bill's co-introducer.
That same day the House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On September 30, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained without action for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2005.
No vote was ever held in either the subcommittee, the full committee, or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage — particularly in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage industries — were better off, because the federal wage floor stayed at $5.15 and workers' real wages kept falling rather than rising to $7.00.

for.name: Rep. Richard Neal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer when it was filed.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill sat, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so the bill went nowhere during the rest of the 108th Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no action on it beyond sending it to a subcommittee; it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support — a Democratic sponsor, co-introducer, and four Democratic cosponsors — and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without a vote.

industries.industry: Low-wage service and retail employers (restaurants, retail, hospitality)
industries.note: The bill raised the wage floor roughly 36% over two years, directly increasing payroll costs for businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage workers. Those costs are passed to customers in small price increases and to owners in thinner margins.

Small employers on thin margins would face the same wage increases as large chains. The bill's phased schedule (three steps over two years) gave them time to adjust, which is the standard concession to this concern.
